section_summary: This section traces Chinese coolie immigration and emigration through Dairen and other Manchurian ports from 1933 through 1936, chiefly through quarterly consular reports and statistical tables. It documents rapid growth in arrivals during 1934, subsequent Japanese and “Manchukuo” restrictions administered through the Tatung labor-certification system, annual quotas, attempted circumvention of controls, and the seasonal movement and earnings of laborers. It also includes a report and translated ordinance on the admission of foreigners to the Kwantung Leased Territory, a Tsingtao report on restricted permits, and tables showing immigrants’ provincial origins and destinations within Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, Second Quarter 1933
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Chinese coolie arrivals and departures through Dairen during the second quarter of 1933.
subfiles.summary: Vincent supplements an earlier report with comparative figures for the second quarter, first half of 1933, and the years 1931–1932. He notes a year-on-year net increase of about 11,000 coolies and regrets that equivalent statistics for Newchwang are unavailable. The enclosure tabulates traffic by port of origin and sex.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, July–September 1933
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits third-quarter 1933 statistics for Chinese migration through Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Vincent's report on Chinese arrivals and departures through Dairen, July-September 1933, from the Kwantung Marine Department, estimates a net increase of 56,000 in nine months, gives partial Newchwang figures, and compares totals with earlier years.

subfiles.title: Department Summary of Dairen’s November 4 Despatch
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes the reported excess of Chinese arrivals over departures at Dairen and Newchwang.
subfiles.summary: Summary of Dairen's November 4 despatch: a nine-month net gain of about 56,000 through Dairen and a much larger surplus of arrivals at Newchwang in March-July 1933.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen and Newchwang, 1933
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reviews 1933 Chinese migration through Dairen and Newchwang and places it in an eleven-year context.
subfiles.summary: Vincent reports a combined net increase of about 188,000 Chinese through Dairen and Newchwang during 1933. He argues that migration reflects employment opportunities rather than approval of the new political regime and identifies construction and agriculture as the principal sources of work. Enclosures provide port-by-port figures for 1933 and annual Manchurian totals for 1923–1933.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, January–March 1934
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a sharp rise in Chinese arrivals through Dairen during the first quarter of 1934.
subfiles.summary: The despatch records 152,874 arrivals and 64,800 departures, for a net increase of 88,074, compared with only 13,824 a year earlier. Vincent suggests that construction rather than agriculture was attracting the additional labor because soybean demand and prices had declined. The enclosure separates traffic by origin, sex, and direction.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, April–June 1934
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports second-quarter 1934 coolie traffic and cumulative first-half totals.
subfiles.summary: Vincent notes over 250,000 arrivals but about 100,000 departures through Dairen in early 1934, thinks construction absorbed more immigrants than farming given few women, and compares the quarter and half-year with 1933 and earlier totals.

subfiles.title: Department Comment on Dairen’s November 1, 1934 Despatch
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Comments on the substantial growth of Chinese immigration to Manchuria in 1934.
subfiles.summary: Comment on Dairen's November 1, 1934 despatch: first-nine-month 1934 net gain of 170,140 against 1933, concluding laborers and peasants, especially from Shantung, learned Manchuria again offered economic advantages.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, July–September 1934
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports third-quarter and cumulative nine-month migration through Dairen in 1934.
subfiles.summary: Although third-quarter arrivals declined from the preceding quarter and from 1933, cumulative 1934 arrivals were almost double those of the corresponding prior period. Vincent reports an incoming surplus of 170,144 for January–September and remarks on the reduced female share. The enclosure gives detailed port and sex statistics.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Copy of Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, July–September 1934
subfiles.doc_type: duplicate consular despatch with statistical enclosure
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Duplicates the November 1 report and table on third-quarter 1934 migration.
subfiles.summary: This is another copy of the despatch found on pages 18–20. It repeats the comparison of 1934 and 1933 arrivals, departures, cumulative gains, and the proportion of women among migrants.

subfiles.title: Special Immigration Reports and Regulations Relative to Foreigners
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.about: Describes rules governing foreign workers and supplies a translation of the 1918 Kwantung foreign-entry ordinance.
subfiles.summary: Entertainers and foreign employees face the same admission standards: not destitute, no coolie labor, no political or communist activity; Russians get closer examination, while firm employment eases entry; the enclosure translates Kwantung Ordinance 15 on passports, exclusion, expulsion, health, enemy nationals and exemptions.

subfiles.title: Duplicate First Page of January 25, 1935 Dairen Migration Despatch
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Duplicate opening page of the annual report on 1934 migration through Dairen and Newchwang.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate first page of the January 25, 1935 Dairen migration despatch, introducing fourth-quarter and annual statistics and Newchwang figures; it breaks off at the page boundary.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen and Newchwang, 1934
subfiles.doc_type: consular despatch with statistical enclosures and press quotation
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reviews fourth-quarter and annual 1934 migration, employment, wages, and laborers’ remittances.
subfiles.summary: Vincent reports 392,009 arrivals and 207,106 departures through Dairen during 1934, while Newchwang showed a much smaller net increase than in 1933. He attributes much immigration to railway and construction projects and cites a press estimate that returning coolies carried 35 million in Manchukuo currency back to China. He assesses seasonal wages and argues that permanent residents probably remitted more money than returning coolies. Enclosures provide detailed Dairen and Newchwang statistics.

subfiles.title: Department Note on Coolie Arrivals and New Regulations
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes the March 23 report on migration controls, February traffic, remittances, and new Manchukuo regulations.
subfiles.summary: Note: police and petty officials tried to restrict departures, about 22,000 arrived in February, annual outflow is estimated at 35 million yen, and new regulations aimed to exclude undesirable or anti-Manchukuo laborers; no action required.

subfiles.title: Coolie Arrivals and Departures through Dairen and New Regulations Thereof
subfiles.doc_type: consular despatch with statistical enclosure and regulatory digest
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports February coolie traffic and emerging controls over Chinese labor immigration.
subfiles.summary: Grummon describes Chinese and Japanese enforcement of Tatung certificates, including the deportation of coolies lacking them, and supplies February arrivals and departures by port and sex. He discusses the 440,000-person quota, shipping-company objections, and the financial concern caused by laborers carrying money home. A press digest outlines new Manchukuo identification rules and categories of excluded laborers, while the enclosure recapitulates annual migration since 1923.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, January–March 1935
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the effect of official restrictions on first-quarter 1935 coolie migration.
subfiles.summary: Grummon: arrivals fell to under half the 1934 figure and the net increase dropped from 88,074 to 20,861, with fewer women showing more seasonal migration and complaints from shipping and press; 29,250 arrived through Newchwang.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, April–June 1935
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports second-quarter 1935 coolie arrivals and departures through Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Arrivals and departures both declined from the corresponding quarter of 1934, although the net increase remained substantial. Grummon finds no major change in the underlying attractions of seasonal farm work and industrial or construction employment. The enclosure breaks down the movement by port, sex, and direction.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, July–September 1935
subfiles.from: Troy L. Perkins, American Vice Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports third-quarter movement and the enforcement of the 440,000-person annual quota.
subfiles.summary: Perkins attributes the quarterly decline mainly to seasons but a sharp September drop to new restrictions: Japanese officials reportedly ordered the Tatung Labor Agency to stop certificates at North China ports as the 440,000 quota neared exhaustion; plans to encourage Japanese settlement in Manchuria are discussed.

subfiles.title: Department Note on the 440,000 Chinese Immigration Limit
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Records the Japanese decision to limit Chinese immigration into Manchuria to 440,000 during 1935.
subfiles.summary: Note: the announced 440,000 ceiling compares with 372,009 immigrants in 1934; about 396,000 had entered by October, and the restrictive policy's permanence was uncertain.

subfiles.title: Department Summary of Tsingtao Despatch No. 64
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Tatung Company’s control over labor certificates for migration from Tsingtao.
subfiles.summary: Summary of Tsingtao Despatch 64: the company, organized in 1934, is Japan's sole certificate issuer; apparent laborers may be excluded without certificates and permits are refused to those lacking definite employment.

subfiles.title: Restriction of Chinese Immigration from Tsingtao to Manchuria
subfiles.from: Samuel Sokobin, American Consul at Tsingtao
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador at Peiping
subfiles.about: Describes the Tatung Company’s restrictive issuance of permits to emigrants bound for Manchuria through Dairen.
subfiles.summary: After a former employee of John Carter Vincent was denied a permit for lacking definite Dairen employment, Sokobin explains the company's fees, photograph rule, Japanese recognition and refusal grounds; a consular employee posing as an emigrant learned it issued only ten or twelve permits daily.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, October–December 1935
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reviews fourth-quarter and annual 1935 coolie migration after the September restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Grummon: the 1935 net increase fell to 71,463 from 164,903 mainly as the Tatung Labor Agency's restrictions cut arrivals; departures softened late in the year from fear of readmission problems; a marine-police estimate says departing coolies carried nearly six million yen.

subfiles.title: Department Note on First-Quarter 1936 Migration
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Notes stable arrivals but reduced departures through Dairen in early 1936.
subfiles.summary: Note: Chinese immigration stayed near the previous year's level in early 1936, with lower departures possibly from reports that reentry into Manchuria would be restricted.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, January–March 1936
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports first-quarter 1936 migration and a substantial decline in departures.
subfiles.summary: Grummon: arrivals nearly unchanged from early 1935, departures down over 10,000, net increase 30,845, low departures again blamed on fear of future exclusion, with unconfirmed reports of a major cut in the 1936 allowable influx.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, April–June 1936
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports second-quarter 1936 traffic and explains how third-class travel distorted official coolie statistics.
subfiles.summary: Reduced third-class fares let many laborers evade Tatung classification, certificate fees and Water Police counting, so reported arrivals understated movement, yet over half of 1935's total entered in early 1936; a North Manchuria labor shortage led highway authorities to use convicts.

subfiles.title: Department Summary of Dairen’s November 6, 1936 Report
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes third-quarter migration and the occupational allocation of the 440,000-person quota.
subfiles.summary: Summary of Dairen's November 6, 1936 report comparing July-September arrivals and departures, with the quota split among farmers, construction workers, miners and coolies and the consulate's expectation it would stabilize Manchuria's Chinese labor force.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, July–September 1936
subfiles.doc_type: consular despatch with four statistical enclosures
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Erle R. Dickover, U.S. diplomatic official at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes third-quarter migration, the 440,000-person control system, and immigrants’ origins and destinations.
subfiles.summary: Grummon reports that the third-class loophole had been closed and treats the current figures as reasonably accurate. He explains the occupational and seasonal allocation of the annual quota and questions whether the timing rules would effectively exclude many farmers. Using the South Manchuria Railway’s Fifth Report of Progress in Manchuria, he compares official datasets and estimates the shares entering through Dairen, Shanhaiguan, Yingkou, and Antung. Four enclosures give quarterly traffic, annual immigration for 1926–1935, provincial origins, and destinations within Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Chinese Immigration and Emigration through Dairen, October–December 1936
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reviews fourth-quarter and annual 1936 coolie traffic and discusses prospective expansion of the immigration quota.
subfiles.summary: Late 1936: arrivals rose modestly, post-harvest departures sharply, both above late 1935; the annual net increase kept falling from the 1934 peak; Grummon concludes 1936's movement nearly filled the quota and industrial expansion might raise it from 400,000 to 600,000.
